I then went behind RPO to the translation's own first edition, Internet Archive poemsros00rossuoft, Rossetti's Poems of 1870, where the piece stands as THE BALLAD OF DEAD LADIES under the heading THREE TRANSLATIONS FROM FRANÇOIS VILLON, 1450, with the same refrain four times and the same hyphen. So there is no drift. The defect is bibliographic, and it is the kind the standard calls the worst failure. The source line reads Rossetti's Complete Poetical Works, p. 237 (trans. Dante Gabriel Rossetti, 1870), which pairs a page out of one book with the year of a different one. There is no 1870 Complete Poetical Works. The Complete Poetical Works is W. M. Rossetti's posthumous edition, Roberts Brothers, 1887, and p. 237 is its page, as the verifier's own evidence field says in as many words; 1870 is the year of Poems, where the translation first appeared, at pp. 177 to 178 of that volume. A reader following the citation as printed looks for p. 237 in a book that does not exist under that year. Rule 4 asks for edition and page, and the edition named is both undated and misdated. Fix it either by dating the edition (Complete Poetical Works, 1887, p. 237) or, cleaner and shorter, by dropping the borrowed page and locating the refrain by line in the 1870 translation, which is what betterCitation does at 107 characters. Nothing else is wrong: attribution to Villon with the translator named is correct for a translated line; the refrain is the sentence the poem is known by; the question mark is allowed; 137 characters, no dash, no straight quote; Poetry is the form; ubi sunt is the August theme exactly; shipped.js returns nothing shipped and nothing near for either Villon or Rossetti, both at 0 of 3, neither banned.
